title: CSC3710 2026-08-20: Languages, Machines, and a Vending-Machine DFA

questions.q: In this course's sense, what is a grammar?
choices: A list of every valid sentence in the language, written out one by one
A concise, exact description of what is in a language
A program that translates source code into machine code
A beginner's tutorial for learning a language
questions.explain: A grammar is a concise, exact description of what is in a language. Think of English grammar, but precise.

questions.q: Using the lecture's example, 'dogs like I' is a sentence in the English language.
questions.explain: 'I like dogs' is in the English language. 'Dogs like I' is not. A language is the set of things that are in it, and this string isn't.

questions.q: What job does a parser do?
choices: It runs the program and reports its output
It translates a valid program into machine code
It takes a file and decides whether it belongs to the language, e.g. whether it is a valid Java program
It writes a grammar by studying example programs
questions.explain: The parser checks membership in the language ('yes, this is Java'). Translating to machine code is the compiler's job, and that comes after the parser.

questions.q: A parser for a programming language is built on the basis of what?
choices: The compiler's output
The computer's hardware
A collection of sample programs
The language's grammar
questions.explain: Parsers are created from the grammar. That is the main real-world reason grammars matter.

questions.q: In the pipeline described in lecture, what happens to a source file once the parser confirms it is a valid Java program?
choices: It is rewritten as a grammar
It is discarded, because checking was the only goal
It is passed on to the compiler
It is handed to a Turing machine to be proven correct
questions.explain: source file -> parser (is this valid Java?) -> if yes -> compiler.

questions.q: The grammar of a programming language defines it exactly, so you could learn to program in that language just by reading its grammar rules.
questions.explain: The grammar rules define the language concisely and exactly, but you wouldn't learn the language from them.

questions.q: A full programming language like Java is complex, so its grammar must be enormous, hundreds of pages long.
questions.explain: The Java grammar fits in about 5 pages. Grammars are very short and exact even for complex languages, and that concise kind of description is what this course cares about.

questions.q: Which statements about languages, grammars, and parsers match the lecture?
choices: A language can be thought of as the set of things that are 'in' it
A given file either is or is not a valid program in a given language
Parsers are built from grammars
A grammar's main purpose is to make programs run faster
The compiler decides whether a file is in the language before the parser ever sees it
questions.explain: A language is a set, and a file is either in it or not. Parsers are built from grammars. The parser does the membership check before the compiler, not after.

questions.q: Under what assumption is an ordinary digital computer considered a Turing machine?
choices: That it has a quantum processor
That it runs only one program at a time
That its memory is unlimited
That it never makes arithmetic errors
questions.explain: Real memory is finite, but we assume we can always add more. With unlimited memory, a digital computer is a Turing machine.

questions.q: When a computer is treated as a Turing machine, the extra memory we assume it can always get has to be random-access memory (RAM).
questions.explain: It doesn't have to be random access. You can just keep adding more disks.

questions.q: It has been proven that no kind of machine more powerful than a Turing machine can exist.
questions.explain: Nobody has come up with a more powerful kind of machine, but that doesn't prove one can't exist.

questions.q: According to the lecture, how do quantum computers compare with Turing machines?
choices: They can solve problems that no Turing machine can solve
They may do some things faster, but they cannot solve any problem a Turing machine can't
They are strictly weaker than Turing machines
They are not models of computation at all
questions.explain: Quantum computers are also Turing machines in this sense. They may be faster at some things, but they solve no problem an ordinary machine couldn't.

questions.q: A traveling salesman problem with a huge number of points, which would take a normal computer thousands of years, still counts as solvable by that computer.
questions.explain: We know the computer will eventually produce the answer. Being slow in practice doesn't make it unsolvable.

questions.q: What distinction does the traveling salesman example illustrate?
choices: Deterministic vs. nondeterministic machines
Grammars vs. parsers
Finite memory vs. unlimited memory
A problem being solvable vs. being solvable quickly
questions.explain: It may take thousands of years, but it will finish. 'Can solve' is a different question from 'can solve quickly.'

questions.q: Which statements are consistent with the lecture?
choices: Nobody has come up with a kind of machine more powerful than the Turing machine
Quantum computers are a more powerful kind of machine than Turing machines, because they can solve more problems
A problem that would take thousands of years to solve is unsolvable
The fact that no more powerful machine has been found does not prove that none exists
Real computers literally have unlimited memory
questions.explain: No more powerful machine is known, but that is not a proof one can't exist. Quantum computers solve no extra problems. Slow is not the same as unsolvable. Unlimited memory is an assumption, not a fact about real computers.

questions.q: In the vending-machine model, what does a state represent?
choices: A single coin
The price of a bottle
How much money has been deposited so far, which is the machine's only memory
A message the machine displays to the customer
questions.explain: A state is what the machine remembers. Here that is the amount deposited so far, e.g. '$0.25 deposited.'

questions.q: What is the initial state of the vending machine?
choices: The state in which a bottle is released
The state the machine is in when it is plugged in, remembering nothing ($0.00 deposited)
Any state that has a self-loop
The state with the most incoming arrows
questions.explain: When you plug the machine in, it starts fresh in the initial state, $0.00 deposited.

questions.q: As the instructor described it, what does it mean for the machine to be deterministic?
choices: There is exactly one final state
Every state has at least one incoming arrow
The machine always ends in the final state
Every state has exactly one outgoing arrow for each input
questions.explain: Deterministic means every state has one arrow for every input. With inputs Q and H, every state needs exactly two outgoing arrows.

questions.q: A DFA has 5 states and 2 input symbols. How many transitions (arrows) must it have in total?
questions.explain: Every state needs one transition per input: 5 x 2 = 10.

questions.q: A DFA has 7 states and an input alphabet of 3 symbols. How many transitions must it have in total?
questions.explain: (number of states) x (number of inputs) = 7 x 3 = 21.

questions.q: A transition is allowed to go from a state back to that same state.
questions.explain: An input can leave the machine in the same state. You draw that as an arrow from the state back to itself, called a self-loop. The vending machine doesn't need any, but they are allowed.

questions.q: The machine reads its state labels, like '$0.25 deposited', to decide where to go next.
questions.explain: State names are only there for us humans. The machine follows the arrows.

questions.q: A finite automaton can move from one state to another on its own, without reading any input.
questions.explain: To move from one state to another, the machine needs an input, here a quarter or a half dollar. There are no free moves.

questions.q: A state diagram has one arrow from state $0.75 to state $1.00+ with both Q and H stacked as labels. How many transitions does that single arrow represent?
questions.explain: When two transitions join the same pair of states, they get drawn as one arrow with both labels. It is still two transitions, one for Q and one for H.

questions.q: In a deterministic machine, a state may have two outgoing arrows with the same input label that go to different states.
questions.explain: Deterministic means exactly one arrow per input from each state, so the next state is never ambiguous.

questions.q: In the vending-machine model, what does the final state (double circle) mean?
choices: The machine shuts off
The bottle of water is released
The machine gives change
The machine rejects the last coin
questions.explain: The final state, '$1.00 or more', marks where the bottle is released. It does not mean the machine stops.

questions.q: Which inputs does the vending machine understand?
choices: Quarters, half dollars, and dollar coins
Any coin worth at least 25 cents
Dimes, quarters, and half dollars
Quarters and half dollars only
questions.explain: The spec says the machine accepts only quarters and half dollars. Anything else, like a dollar coin, is outside the model.

questions.q: How many states does the vending-machine DFA built in class have?
Why does the design use a separate '$1.00 or more' state instead of making $0.00 the final state and sending the $1 arrows back to it?
choices: A state can never be both initial and final
If the initial state were also final, plugging the machine in would release a bottle
A DFA may have only one state with incoming arrows
$0.00 already has too many outgoing arrows
questions.explain: The machine starts in the initial state, and the final state means 'bottle released.' If $0.00 were both, you'd get a bottle just by plugging the machine in. So the release state has to be one you can reach only by inserting money.

questions.q: From the '$1.00 or more' state, where does a quarter take the machine?
choices: '$1.00 or more' (a self-loop)
questions.explain: The next coin starts a new count from zero, so a quarter means $0.25 has been deposited toward the next bottle.

questions.q: Suppose the final state's quarter arrow went to $0.00 instead. What would go wrong?
choices: The machine would no longer be deterministic
The customer's next quarter would be eaten, taken without giving any credit
The machine would release two bottles at once
The machine would start giving change
questions.explain: Following an arrow uses up the coin. Going to $0.00 means the quarter was taken and nothing was credited. (The machine would still be deterministic, since each state would still have one arrow per input.)

questions.q: The machine is in state $0.75 and a customer inserts a half dollar. Where does it go?
choices: A new $1.25 state
$0.25, after giving back a quarter in change
'$1.00 or more'
It stays in $0.75 because the coin is too much
questions.explain: $1.25 reaches or exceeds $1, and the machine gives no change, so it lands in '$1.00 or more' and releases the bottle.

questions.q: The machine is in state $0.25 and a customer inserts a half dollar. Where does it go?
choices: '$1.00 or more'
$0.25 (a self-loop)

questions.q: The design needs a separate '$1.25' state for when a customer overpays.
questions.explain: The spec says 'reaches or exceeds $1.' With no change given, $1.00 and $1.25 behave exactly the same, so they share one state.

questions.q: If a customer puts in exactly two half dollars, the machine gets stuck in the final state and can't be used again.
questions.explain: The bottle is released and the machine sits in '$1.00 or more.' The next coin moves it to $0.25 or $0.50 and starts a new purchase. Being in the final state doesn't mean the machine has stopped.

questions.q: The 5-state diagram built in class is the only correct DFA for this vending machine.
questions.explain: Many designs are valid. You can always model the same behavior with more states than you need. A correct machine just has to behave right and be deterministic.

questions.q: Which of these changes would make the vending-machine design wrong?
choices: Making $0.00 both the initial and the final state
Sending the final state's quarter arrow back to $0.00
Giving $0.75 an arrow for Q but none for H
Using short state labels so they fit inside the circles
Adding transitions for dimes
questions.explain: Initial-and-final releases a bottle on plug-in. An arrow back to $0.00 eats the next coin. A missing arrow breaks determinism. Dimes aren't an input this machine accepts. Short labels are fine, since the labels are only for humans.

questions.q: Redesign the machine for a bottle that costs $0.75, with the same coins (quarters and half dollars) and still no change. What is the fewest number of states you need?
questions.explain: $0.00 (initial), $0.25, $0.50, and '$0.75 or more' (final).

questions.q: In that $0.75-bottle redesign, where does the $0.50 state go on a quarter?
choices: '$0.75 or more' (final)
$0.50 (a self-loop)
questions.explain: $0.50 + $0.25 = $0.75, which reaches the price, so the machine moves to the final state and releases a bottle.

questions.q: Starting from $0.00, the coins Q H H Q are inserted. Which state does the machine end in, and how many bottles come out?
choices: '$1.00 or more'; 1 bottle
$0.25; 1 bottle
$0.00; 1 bottle
$0.25; 2 bottles

questions.q: Starting from $0.00, the coins H H H H are inserted. How many bottles come out?
Starting from $0.00, which coin sequence leaves the machine in the final state?
choices: H H Q
Q H Q H
Q Q H
Q H
questions.explain: Q Q H: $0.00 -> $0.25 -> $0.50 -> $1.00+. H H Q ends in $0.25, Q H Q H ends in $0.50, and Q H ends in $0.75.

questions.q: Starting from $0.00, a customer inserts Q H H and gets one bottle. How much did they pay in total, in dollars?
questions.explain: $0.25 + $0.50 + $0.50 = $1.25. The last half dollar takes $0.75 to '$1.00 or more,' and the machine gives no change.

questions.q: Starting from $0.00, the coins H Q H Q H are inserted. Which state does the machine end in?
choices: '$1.00 or more'

questions.q: Starting from $0.00, a customer inserts eight quarters in a row. How many bottles come out?
questions.explain: Q Q Q Q reaches $1.00+ (bottle 1). The fifth quarter goes to $0.25, and quarters 6-8 reach $1.00+ again (bottle 2).

questions.q: Starting from $0.00, the coins Q H Q H are inserted. Which state does the machine end in?
choices: '$1.00 or more'

questions.q: Starting from $0.00, a customer inserts six quarters in a row. How many bottles come out?
questions.explain: Four quarters reach $1.00+ (bottle). The fifth quarter goes to $0.25 and the sixth to $0.50, which isn't enough for a second bottle.

questions.q: Starting from $0.00, the coins Q H H H H are inserted. Where does the machine end, and how many bottles come out?
choices: $0.50; 1 bottle
'$1.00 or more'; 2 bottles
'$1.00 or more'; 1 bottle
$0.75; 2 bottles
